title: Hand hygiene disparities between healthcare and non-healthcare students: Implications for cross-disciplinary public health education
content:
by Laia Selva-Pareja, Carla Camí, Judith Roca, Olga Masot, Xavier Gómez-Arbonés, Eva Barallat-Gimeno, Alba Torné-Ruiz, Elena Paraíso-Pueyo, Rosa-Mar Alzuria-Alós, Anna Espart

Hand hygiene (HH) is a technique known worldwide to be effective in reducing the spread of communicable diseases. Despite widespread public information campaigns in recent years, proper knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAPs) regarding HH may still be inconsistent among young adults. This study aimed to analyze these KAPs in two comparable groups—healthcare and non-healthcare university students—to identify disparities and inform public health education strategies. Students were invited to complete an ad hoc online questionnaire, adapted from previously published instruments. A total of 457 university students participated in this cross-sectional study, 55.6% of whom were healthcare students. Of all students, 80.5% indicated having sufficient knowledge to perform correct HH—90.6% of healthcare students and 68.0% of non-healthcare students. Most participants identified soap and water and alcohol-based hand rub as effective hand hygiene agents. Significant differences were observed between groups in the use of hand hygiene agents, with healthcare students showing more appropriate practices. Although both groups reported regular use of soap and water, differences emerged in specific hygiene routines. Multivariate analysis showed that being a healthcare student was independently associated with better HH-related knowledge, attitudes, and practices. In conclusion, integrating structured hand hygiene education across university curricula may help reduce behavioral gaps and strengthen infection prevention beyond healthcare disciplines.
